from pathlib import Path
import re, statistics
s=Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').read_text()
p13=s.split('===== PAGE 13 =====')[1].split('===== PAGE 14 =====')[0]
rows=[]
for line in p13.splitlines():
    m=re.match(r'"'^(.*?)'"\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(-?\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+(\\d+\\.\\d+)\\s+',line)
    if m:
        rows.append((m[1],*[float(m[i]) for i in range(2,6)]))
print('Occupation rows',len(rows))
for label,r in [('Male-stereotyped',rows[:20]),('Female-stereotyped',rows[20:]),('Overall',rows)]:
    print(label,'SS single',statistics.mean(x[1] for x in r),'SS paired',statistics.mean(x[3] for x in r),'mean abs SS single',statistics.mean(abs(x[1]) for x in r))
p15=s.split('===== PAGE 15 =====')[1]
power=[]
for line in p15.splitlines():
    m=re.match(r'"'^(.*?) (minor|power) (-?'"\\d+\\.\\d+) (-?\\d+\\.\\d+) (-?\\d+\\.\\d+)"'$'"',line)
    if m:
        power.append((m[1],m[2],float(m[3]),float(m[4])))
print('Power rows',len(power))
for label,r in [('Low power',[x for x in power if x[1]=='minor']),('High power',[x for x in power if x[1]=='power']),('Overall',power)]:
    print(label,'SS single',statistics.mean(x[2] for x in r),'SS paired',statistics.mean(x[3] for x in r))
for name,ss,both,any_ in [('Occupation',47.38,71.9,74.3),('Power',18.98,57.9,59.7)]:
    print(name, 'stereotyped person percentage from SS', (100+ss)/2,'stereotyped person percentage from figure 4',(both+any_)/2,'implied any percentage',ss+100-both)
PY"

strengths: PST addresses a relevant multimodal NLP question: whether gender stereotypes become more pronounced when models generate two people together. Studying organizational power alongside occupation adds a useful perspective.

The occupational experiment systematically covers 800 ordered combinations of 20 male-stereotyped and 20 female-stereotyped occupations, including both left/right orders. The paired SS of 47.38 provides substantial evidence of stereotype adherence in the tested DALL-E 3 setting.

Three human annotations per image, reported Fleiss’ kappa of 0.88–0.92, explicit annotation instructions, and detailed occupation-level results strengthen the empirical contribution. Checking automated annotation against humans and reporting its poor performance is also valuable.
weaknesses: The central fairness interpretation exceeds what the signed SS establishes. Opposing disparities can cancel: Table 2 averages female-stereotyped occupation SS of 50 and male-stereotyped occupation SS of −30 into an apparently small overall score of 10. This does not establish that single-person generation approaches the stated equal-representation ideal. Similarly, Figure 4’s percentage with any stereotypical individual requires a chance baseline: independent, gender-balanced assignments would produce at least one stereotypical individual in 75% of pairs. The results support increased stereotype alignment more clearly than the broader fair-versus-biased framing.

The comparative sampling is weak for several conclusions. Single-person occupational estimates use only three images per occupation, versus 40 appearances per occupation in PST. No confidence intervals or analysis accounting for shared occupations and paired individuals is supplied. Occupation-specific amplification rankings are consequently uncertain. Organizational-power comparisons also need clearer documentation of how sampled roles are matched across conditions.

Annotation reliability does not establish that the generated people satisfy the requested occupations, power roles, and positions. No systematic DALL-E 3 instruction-adherence audit is reported. Appendix C permits 'Cannot Identify', but its treatment, disagreement resolution, and resulting denominators are unspecified. Reproducibility is further limited by missing generation dates, access-interface details, and treatment of any prompt rewriting; code and generated data are only promised upon acceptance.

The mitigation conclusions are too broad for one intervention, with occupational testing restricted to the five most biased occupations per gender. Selection effects and sampling uncertainty are not assessed. In particular, an organizational-power SS of −11.12 without an uncertainty estimate does not establish reliable reverse stereotyping. These experiments support an exploratory DALL-E 3 case study, but not general conclusions about the controllability of prompt-based mitigation.

Reported quantities need reconciliation. Section 3.2.2 states 944 prompts, whereas its component counts total 1,952. Under the stated binary two-person evaluation, Figure 4’s occupational 'Both' and 'Any' percentages imply 73.1% stereotypical individuals, while Table 2’s SS implies 73.69%; the denominators are not explained. The credible core observation makes Findings plausible, but the metric interpretation, evaluation documentation, and uncertainty concerns prevent a clear positive recommendation.
